Canonical Hours
kuh-NON-ih-kul OWRZ
n. pl. (the seven or eight fixed times of daily prayer appointed by church rule)
Greek kanon, a measuring rod or rule, through Latin canonicus, according to rule; with hora, an hour. Hours measured out by rule.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The canonical hours are the fixed times of prayer appointed by ecclesiastical rule: matins and lauds before dawn, prime at the first hour, terce at the third, sext at the sixth, none at the ninth, vespers at evening and compline at bedtime. The division is older than the monasteries that perfected it. Scripture itself marks the hours of prayer — “the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1), and Peter praying “about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9); the Psalmist keeps “Evening, and morning, and at noon” (Psa 55:17); and the night watches have their own office in “all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD” (Psa 134:1). A Christian who sets times to pray is walking in a very old and very good path. What the word canonical added was obligation: these hours by rule, their omission a fault requiring confession, their recitation a debt to the church. That is where Scripture parts company with the system. The rule may order a house; it may not bind a conscience as though God had commanded it. Fixed hours are a servant of prayer and a tyrant the moment they are made its measure.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines canonical as pertaining to a canon, according to the ecclesiastical canons, and notes canonical hours as certain stated times of the day appropriated to prayer; and hour as the twenty-fourth part of a day.

expand to see more

CANONICAL, a. Pertaining to a canon; according to the canon or rule.

CANONICAL HOURS, certain stated times of the day, fixed by ecclesiastical laws, or appropriated to the offices of prayer and devotion.

HOUR, n. A space of time equal to the twenty fourth part of the natural day; sixty minutes.

CANON, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign.

STATED, a. Settled; established; regular; occurring at regular times.

Key Scripture

Act 3:1 — "Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour."

Act 10:9 — "On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour:"

Psa 55:17 — "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice."

Psa 134:1 — "A Song of degrees. Behold, bless ye the LORD, all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD."

Modern Corruption

Fixed times of prayer by church rule: a good scaffold turned into an obligation, and lately into a productivity schedule with the prayer taken out.

expand to see more

The historic corruption is the word canonical itself. Setting times to pray is wisdom; decreeing them under pain of sin is to legislate where God has not spoken, and Paul met the same spirit in men who would judge a brother by a calendar. Christ's own practice is instructive and free: “in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35) — an hour kept, not an hour owed.

The modern misuse keeps the grid and discards the Object. Fixed hours are now recommended for focus, circadian hygiene and the management of attention, and the recommendation is often sound as far as it goes; it simply is not prayer. The principle to recover is that an hour is holy because of who is addressed in it, not because of where it falls in the day: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee” (Psa 5:3).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kanon (G2583), a rule; Greek hora (G5610), an hour; Hebrew eth (H6256), a set time; Hebrew tamid (H8548), continual; Greek kairos (G2540), a season.

expand to see more

Greek kanon (G2583) — a measuring rod, hence a rule or standard; the root of “canonical” and of “canon”.

Greek hora (G5610) — an hour; “the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1).

Hebrew eth (H6256) — a set or appointed time, the hour fixed for a thing.

Hebrew tamid (H8548) — continual, the word of the daily sacrifice morning and evening.

Greek kairos (G2540) — a season or opportune moment, time regarded by its fitness rather than its length.

Usage

"“Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9) — an apostle keeping an hour, with no rule compelling him."

"“which by night stand in the house of the LORD” (Psa 134:1) — the night office has a biblical warrant the obligation never had."

"“From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD” (Psa 113:3) — the day bounded by praise rather than carved into debts."
